newsitem.title: UK: Victorious Labour gears up to deliver mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Victorious Labour gears up to deliver mini-budget.

text.p: Fresh from a stunning election victory, one of the first tasks of the new British Labour government will be preparing a mini-budget within months.

Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer-in-waiting Gordon Brown said on Friday a budget will be held within two months to implement the windfall tax on privatised utilities, the proceeds of which will help 250,000 young people into work.
Labour's first budget will also cut value added tax on fuel to five percent from eight, Brown said.

But while Labour has pledged to keep the main rates of income tax unchanged for the lifetime of the parliament, economists are starting to focus on the possibility of other tax rises to improve shaky public finances.
Economists said Labour can simply turn to backdoor taxes if it wants to spend more.
"There are plenty of ways for an incoming Labour government to raise revenue without changing income tax rates," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

With over 200 tax exemptions, reliefs and allowances in the tax system to choose from, the party has room for manoeuvre despite the promise to leave alone main income tax rates, which have not risen since 1977.

Labour has also pledged to stick to public spending targets set by the Conservative government for the first two years of the next parliament -- a clear effort to demonstrate how fiscally frugal the party has become.

But analysts said Britain's high level of public debt after four strong years of economic growth, coupled with the need to re-balance demand in the economy away from the consumer, could make fiscal tightening tempting for a new Labour government, even in its first budget.

British voters have been mesmerised for decades by the main rates of income tax, and applauded sharp cuts delivered by Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, particularly in 1988 when the top rate of tax fell to 40 percent from 60 percent.
But the Conservatives, who had held power since 1979, have relied heavily on backdoor tax increases -- such as restricting the value of tax allowances -- to raise revenue.
"The Conservatives raised 17 billion pounds ($28 billion) in 1993 budgets without touching the main income tax rates once," said Chris Giles, economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
Those tax rises, as Labour has argued, were equivalent to putting over seven pencentage points on the basic rate of income tax.

So while on the face of it Labour may have made a historic break with its tax-and-spend past, analysts said the move may be more symbolic than real. The party will still be able to embrace a more redistributive and progressive tax system, but much less aggressively than in the 1970s or 1960s when redistribution of wealth was high on the party's agenda.

"Labour are clearly aiming for at least two terms in office," said Lyons of DKB. "The party produced a programme first to woo the floating voter, woo the financial markets, and then, further down the line, woo the traditional Labour supporter."

Now it has won power, Labour is spoiled for choice on tax-raising measures. It could scrap tax relief on mortgage interest payments (raising 2.4 billion pounds), the married couples' allowance (2.8 billion) or the tax credit on advance corporation tax (5.0 billion).

But, significantly, Labour's tax pledges mean it will not be able to "squeeze the rich until the pips squeak," as Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer Dennis Healey promised during the last Labour government in the 1970s.
The top rate of income tax will stay at 40 percent and fiddling with tax allowances does not significantly affect the incomes of very high earners, who did not panic ahead of the general election.

The rich may escape relatively unscathed but there could be casualties in the next public spending round, with the party forced to take an ultra-tough line against government departments which will be pushing for extra money from the new government.

The spending targets over the next two fiscal years are far tougher than those achieved since the 1992 election, and the new Labour government with pledges on health and education may be in for a rough ride, not least from its traditional bugbear -- strong public sector unions, which have a loyal following among many Labour rank-and-file members, economists said.

"Labour wants to examine departmental spending but in truth this will have to involve cuts in services," warns Giles of the IFS. "The public spending round could get nasty." Many think the tough spending targets will not be met, and money will have to be found to balance the books.
